body: One 97 Communications (Paytm) raised Rs 18,300 cr at Rs 2,150/share in Nov 2021 (then India's largest IPO; ~Rs 10,000 cr was offer-for-sale by existing holders). It listed at Rs 1,950 on 18 Nov 2021 and closed at Rs 1,564 (-27%), the worst mainboard debut by size. By Nov 2022 it was ~79% below issue (~Rs 440s). In Mar 2022 RBI barred Paytm Payments Bank (an associate) from onboarding customers; on 31 Jan 2024 RBI ordered PPBL to stop most deposit/credit business from Feb-Mar 2024 citing 'persistent non-compliances', and the stock hit back-to-back 20% lower circuits to ~Rs 300-440 range (exact low unverified). It later recovered substantially as losses narrowed (2024-25). Visible flags at IPO: (1) loss-making since inception with no clear path to profit; (2) valuation ~50x sales-ish on a payments business with near-zero UPI margins; (3) big OFS = insiders selling; (4) QIB book subscribed only ~2.8x; (5) Macquarie's pre-listing Rs 1,200 target (-44%); (6) regulatory dependence on a related payments bank. Lesson: IPOs where insiders sell most of the issue at peak private valuations have poor base rates; regulator actions on a related entity are a key risk. Not a fraud -- a valuation and regulatory blowup, partly reversed.

data.early_signals: loss-making; huge OFS; weak QIB demand; Macquarie target; RBI actions on PPBL 2022
data.lesson: Avoid IPOs priced at last private round with heavy OFS; check regulatory dependence

title: Paytm IPO (Nov 2021): story stock, not fraud

body: THE GOOD NUMBER: Valeant reported fast-rising 'cash EPS' and revenue, run by a McKinsey-trained CEO who cut R&D to ~3% of sales; Pershing Square and Sequoia Fund owned it; the stock peaked ~$262 (Aug 2015). WHY IT LIED: (1) the growth was acquired, not organic: dozens of deals financed with ~$30 bn of debt (debt/EBITDA ~5-7x); (2) 'cash EPS' excluded acquisition and restructuring costs that recurred every year because buying companies was the business model; (3) revenue growth came from price increases (e.g., Syprine +3,000%) rather than volumes, inviting political backlash; (4) an undisclosed specialty pharmacy, Philidor, which Valeant had an option to buy, pushed its drugs. After Citron's Oct-2015 report and Philidor's exposure, the stock fell >90%; renamed Bausch Health. TEST: separate organic from acquired growth; add back 'one-time' costs that recur; check GAAP EPS and FCF after acquisitions; ask whether price or volume drives sales. Buffett's warning on high-P/E acquirers manufacturing EPS applies (insight:buffett-conglomerate-chain-letter-2014). LESSON: EPS growth that needs a continuous flow of debt-financed deals is a financing story, not a compounding business.

data.good_number: rapid growth in adjusted 'cash EPS' and revenue; star investors; low R&D cost base
data.test_that_catches_it: organic volume growth; GAAP vs non-GAAP gap; debt/EBITDA; price vs volume; related distribution channels
data.why_misleading: growth was bought with ~$30 bn of debt and price hikes; recurring acquisition costs were excluded from 'cash EPS'; an undisclosed pharmacy (Philidor) channelled sales

title: Hidden trap: Valeant's 'cash EPS' growth from acquisitions
